scenes.line1: Why does Java speed up after a while?
scenes.say: Ever notice your Java app runs faster after a few loops? Let's see why the Java Virtual Machine needs a warm-up phase.

scenes.label: Hotspots
scenes.sub: JVM finds hot code and compiles it to native instructions at runtime.
scenes.say: The Java Virtual Machine watches for code that runs a lot—these are hotspots. It then compiles this bytecode into fast native instructions while your app is running.

Here's how it works: First, the Java Virtual Machine starts and runs your code in basic mode. Next, it profiles which parts run the most, then compiles those to native code. After that, your app hits peak speed.

scenes.title: See JIT Compilation Logs
scenes.say: You can see this in action by enabling JIT compilation logs when you run your app. You'll see which methods get compiled as the Java Virtual Machine optimizes your code.

scenes.question: Can you benchmark Java code right away?
scenes.right: No, you need a warm-up for the Java Virtual Machine to optimize your code first.
scenes.say: Here's a common trap: If you benchmark Java code without a warm-up, your results will be misleading. Always let the Java Virtual Machine optimize before measuring performance.
